subject: chemistry
question_text: Balance the reaction Cr₂O₇²⁻ + NO₂⁻ → Cr³⁺ + NO₃⁻ in acid medium.

verification.note: Chapter 5 (Stoichiometry) is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.66-72), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. This chapter has NO Long Answer section in the book, so no 8-mark form is invented. The 1+1+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The final equation was independently re-checked: atoms Cr 2=2, N 3=3, O 13=13, H 8=8; charge +3 on each side. AI chemistry check 2026-08-25. Corrected the s1 why: per-atom changes of 2 and 3 alone would give multipliers 3 and 2; the stated 3 and 1 need the TWO chromium atoms (6 electrons). No marked line changed.

steps.label: Identifying the two half reactions
lines: N in NO₂⁻ is +3 → +5 in NO₃⁻ : oxidation
Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻ is +6 → +3 in Cr³⁺ : reduction
steps.why: Nitrogen's oxidation number rises by 2, and each of the two chromium atoms falls by 3, so the dichromate half takes six electrons in all. That fixes the two halves and, later, the multipliers 3 and 1.
common_mistakes: Mislabelling the halves. Dichromate is the oxidising agent, so it is itself reduced.
Computing N in NO₂⁻ as +4. With two O at −2 and charge −1, nitrogen is +3.
steps.memory_tip: Nitrite +3 to nitrate +5; dichromate +6 to chromium +3. Write the numbers over the atoms first.
steps.margin_note: Both skeleton halves with their oxidation-number changes earn this mark.

steps.label: Balanced oxidation half
lines: Balance O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻:
steps.why: One extra oxygen turns nitrite into nitrate, supplied by water; the two freed hydrogens leave as H⁺ and the charge check fixes two electrons on the product side.
common_mistakes: Placing the electrons on the reactant side of an oxidation half.
Forgetting the 2H⁺, which breaks the hydrogen count.
steps.memory_tip: Order in acid: other atoms, O with H₂O, H with H⁺, charge with e⁻.
steps.margin_note: Equation (1) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Balanced reduction half
steps.why: Both chromium atoms drop from +6 to +3, so the half consumes six electrons — three per chromium — and the charge check confirms six.
common_mistakes: Writing 3e⁻ for one chromium and forgetting the ion carries two.
steps.memory_tip: Dichromate in acid is always Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O — it repeats across this chapter.
steps.margin_note: Equation (2) with its charge check earns this mark.

steps.label: Adding and the final equation
lines: Add (2) and cancel 6H⁺ and 3H₂O from both sides:
Check: Cr 2=2, N 3=3, O 13=13, H 8=8; charge +3 = +3
steps.why: Tripling the nitrite half brings both halves to six electrons, so they cancel on addition; cancelling the shared H⁺ and H₂O leaves the simplest equation.
common_mistakes: Leaving 14H⁺ and 7H₂O uncancelled in the final line.
Multiplying the dichromate half by 3 as well.
steps.memory_tip: Electron counts 2 and 6: only the smaller half is tripled — one multiplication.
steps.margin_note: The boxed equation with the atom and charge check earns this mark.

insider_note: The reduction half Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H₂O is a stock line the examiner knows by sight — reproduce it exactly and the question is mostly done.
